text: Starting out on the biography of my hero, Alexei Fyodorovich Karamazov, I find myself in some perplexity.
explanation: The narrator begins with uncertainty and admits he is not fully confident about how to present Alexei's life.

text: Namely, that while I do call Alexei Fyodorovich my hero, still, I myself know that he is by no means a great man, so that I can foresee the inevitable questions, such as: What is notable about your Alexei Fyodorovich that you should choose him for your hero?
explanation: He calls Alexei the hero, but immediately admits Alexei is not obviously great, so readers may question that choice.

text: What has he really done?
explanation: The narrator imagines readers asking what concrete achievements Alexei has.

text: To whom is he known, and for what?
explanation: The question shifts to Alexei's reputation and whether anyone has reason to care about him.

text: Why should I, the reader, spend my time studying the facts of his life?
explanation: The narrator anticipates resistance from readers who are unsure the story is worth their attention.

text: This last question is the most fateful one, for I can only reply: perhaps you will see from the novel.
explanation: He admits the only defense is that the novel itself may eventually justify Alexei's importance.

text: But suppose they read the novel and do not see, do not agree with the noteworthiness of my Alexei Fyodorovich?
explanation: The narrator worries that even after reading, people may still reject his claim that Alexei matters.

text: I say this because, to my sorrow, I foresee it.
explanation: He expects that skeptical reaction and says so with regret.

text: To me he is noteworthy, but I decidedly doubt that I shall succeed in proving it to the reader.
explanation: The narrator believes in Alexei's significance personally, but doubts he can persuade others.

text: The thing is that he does, perhaps, make a figure, but a figure of an indefinite, indeterminate sort.
explanation: Alexei may be meaningful, but not in a clear or easily defined way.

text: Though it would be strange to demand clarity from people in a time like ours.
explanation: The narrator broadens the point and says confusion is natural in a confused age.

text: One thing, perhaps, is rather doubtless: he is a strange man, even an odd one.
explanation: If nothing else is certain, Alexei is at least unusual.

text: But strangeness and oddity will sooner harm than justify any claim to attention, especially when everyone is striving to unite particulars and find at least some general sense in the general senselessness.
explanation: Oddity usually makes a person harder to accept, especially when society wants order and common meaning.

text: Whereas an odd man is most often a particular and isolated case.
explanation: An eccentric person is usually treated as an exception, not as someone central.

text: Is that not so?
explanation: The narrator pauses and asks the reader to agree with that idea.

text: Now if you do not agree with this last point and reply: 'Not so' or 'Not always,' then perhaps I shall take heart concerning the significance of my hero, Alexei Fyodorovich.
explanation: If the reader rejects the idea that odd people are always isolated, the narrator feels more hopeful about Alexei's importance.

text: For not only is an odd man 'not always' a particular and isolated case, but, on the contrary, it sometimes happens that it is precisely he, perhaps, who bears within himself the heart of the whole, while the other people of his epoch have all for some reason been torn away from it for a time by some kind of flooding wind.
explanation: Sometimes the strange person actually carries the essential truth of an era, while everyone else has drifted away from it.

text: I would not, in fact, venture into these rather vague and uninteresting explanations but would simply begin without any introduction, if they like it, they'll read it as it is, but the trouble is that while I have just one biography, I have two novels.
explanation: The narrator says he would rather skip the preface, but the structure of the story forces him to explain himself.

text: The main novel is the second one, about the activities of my hero in our time, that is, in our present, current moment.
explanation: He clarifies that the real focus is the second novel, which covers Alexei in the present.

text: As for the first novel, it already took place thirteen years ago and is even almost not a novel at all but just one moment from my hero's early youth.
explanation: The first novel is more like a background episode from Alexei's earlier life.

text: It is impossible for me to do without this first novel, or much in the second novel will be incomprehensible.
explanation: The narrator insists the earlier material is necessary for understanding what comes later.

text: Thus my original difficulty becomes even more complicated: for if I, that is, the biographer himself, think that even one novel may, perhaps, be unwarranted for such a humble and indefinite hero, then how will it look if I appear with two; and what can explain such presumption on my part?
explanation: His justification problem gets worse because he is asking readers to accept not one book about Alexei, but two.

text: Being at a loss to resolve these questions, I am resolved to leave them without any resolution.
explanation: He gives up trying to settle the issue neatly.

text: To be sure, the keen-sighted reader will already have guessed long ago that that is what I've been getting at from the very beginning and will only be annoyed with me for wasting fruitless words and precious time.
explanation: The narrator knows attentive readers may be irritated because his preface only circles around unresolved doubts.

text: To this I have a ready answer: I have been wasting fruitless words and precious time, first, out of politeness, and, second, out of cunning.
explanation: He jokingly defends the preface as partly courteous and partly strategic.

text: At least I have given some warning beforehand.
explanation: He says the introduction has at minimum served as a warning to readers.

text: In fact, I am even glad that my novel broke itself into two stories while preserving the essential unity of the whole, having acquainted himself with the first story, the reader can decide for himself whether it is worth his while to begin the second.
explanation: He sees an advantage in the split structure because readers can test the first part before deciding to continue.

text: Of course, no one is bound by anything; he can also drop the book after two pages of the first story and never pick it up again.
explanation: Readers are free to abandon the book at any point.

text: But still there are readers of such delicacy that they will certainly want to read to the very end so as to make no mistake in their impartial judgment.
explanation: Some readers will continue out of fairness and seriousness.

text: Such, for instance, are all Russian critics.
explanation: The narrator adds a dry, slightly ironic example: literary critics.

text: Faced with these people, I feel easier in my heart: for, in spite of their care and conscientiousness, I am nonetheless providing them with the most valid pretext for dropping the story at the first episode of the novel.
explanation: He is relieved because even conscientious readers now have a legitimate excuse to stop early if they want.

text: Well, that is the end of my introduction.
explanation: The narrator formally closes the preface.

text: I quite agree that it is superfluous, but since it is already written, let it stand.
explanation: He admits the introduction may be unnecessary, but keeps it anyway.

text: And now to business.
explanation: The narrator finally moves from preface to the real story.
